At 1:15 every day, the bank's staff room clears out and Rukmini stays behind with a sandwich and a yellow sticky pad. Trisha, new to the branch, watched her for a week before asking.

"What's the timer for?"

"Worry window," Rukmini said. "Fifteen minutes. I write everything that's bugging me." She turned the pad around. New regional manager visiting. Leak above my bedroom window. Did I lock the cash drawer properly yesterday. Sister's college results.

Next to two items she had drawn a small tick. "These I can do something about. The leak, I'll call the building office today. The drawer, I'll check the log at two." The others had a little cloud. "These go back in the window tomorrow. Outside it, I don't chew on them."

"Does that work?"

"Mostly. Before, I spent the whole afternoon half here." The timer beeped. Rukmini folded the note into her diary and picked up the phone.

qa.a: At 1:15 every day the staff room clears out.

qa.q: Why does the worry window make Rukmini feel steadier at work?

qa.a: At first Trisha probably found it curious, maybe odd; after the explanation Trisha may see it as a practical skill worth trying.

Hi Sangeeta,

You asked how I'm handling the move to Hyderabad without losing my mind. Honestly, I was losing it. Every night at 2 a.m. my brain ran the list: the new team, the flat, whether Papa will manage the stairs at home without me, whether I'll make any friends.

So I tried something my cousin swore by. Every evening at seven I sit with tea and a notebook for exactly fifteen minutes. I write every worry. Then I put an S next to the ones I can solve. Yesterday the S ones were "book the packers" and "ask the landlord about a gas connection". I did the first one right away.

The rest, like friends and Papa, I leave in the notebook. If they come at 2 a.m., I tell myself: seven o'clock tomorrow.

It isn't magic. But I slept six hours straight last night, first time in weeks.

Write soon,
Urmila

Tarun, you asked how I got through planning my brother's wedding while working full time. I'll tell you, because for about a month I did not get through it well.

I'm Urmila, by the way, the sister who ended up doing everything. The caterer, the relatives from Nagpur, the rain forecast, what if the hall double-booked. I worried in the shower, in meetings, in the auto.

Then my manager, of all people, said, "Give your worries an appointment." So I did. Every morning, 8:30 to 8:45, on the office terrace. I'd write everything. I'd circle what I could act on that day, maybe calling the hall to confirm in writing. I'd do that one thing before ten.

Rain forecast? Not solvable. Relatives' moods? Not solvable. Those stayed on the page until tomorrow's 8:30.

I won't pretend I was calm at the wedding. But I was there. I danced.

qa.a: Every morning, 8:30 to 8:45, on the office terrace.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference in Urmila's approach, and why?
qa.a: Circling what could be acted on and doing that one thing before ten mattered most, because it turned worry into progress while unsolvable items waited.

Coach's note, junior athletics, Friday

Chetan came fifth in the 400 metres today. He had been sure of a medal. At the finish he walked straight to the fence, pulled his cap down and cried hard.

I stood next to Chetan and didn't talk at first. When he looked up I said, "You really wanted this one." He said, "I'm the worst." I told him I'd seen him run his best time at the second bend, and that fifth out of twelve was a real race.

He ran it well and came back grinning. I've told his parents about both races, the tears and the relay.

Sachin

The student council results went up on the corridor board in Oslo on a grey Tuesday. Priscila's name was third out of three.

Anders found her by the lockers. "Hey. You okay?"

She almost said, "Yeah, fine, whatever." It was on her tongue. Instead she took a breath. "Actually, no. I'm disappointed. And kind of embarrassed. I gave that speech in front of everyone and I got the fewest votes."

Anders nodded slowly. "That makes sense. I'd feel the same."

Saying it out loud made her throat loosen. She could feel her face cooling down. They walked to the canteen, and by the time they'd queued for waffles she was able to joke that at least now she had Tuesday afternoons free.

That evening she watched a clip of her speech. It was better than she'd remembered. She wrote down two things she'd change if she ran again next year.

qa.a: The results went up on the corridor board in Oslo on a grey Tuesday.

qa.a: Priscila felt disappointed and embarrassed, since she had given a speech in front of everyone and got the fewest votes.

The under-16 football list was pinned up at the club office at six. Charu read it twice. Her name wasn't there.

In the changing room, Kishore sir was stacking cones. "Charu? Seen the list?"

"Yes, sir." She laced her boots very tightly. "It's fine."

He waited.

She pulled the lace harder, then let go. "No, it isn't fine. I'm really disappointed. And I'm embarrassed, because I told my whole class I'd make it."

"Thank you for telling me that," Kishore sir said. "Both of those make sense."

Something in her chest unknotted. She sat down on the bench. "What do I need to work on?"

"Your left foot, mostly. And you drop back too early. Both fixable by next season."

She walked home slower than usual, but she ate dinner, and she told her mother the truth about the list instead of pretending she hadn't checked.

Hrithik, come, put your phone down a minute. You've been quiet all week, and it reminds your old grandpa of something.

When I was fifteen, the year the mill shut and your great-grandfather lost his job, I stopped doing homework. I sat at the back. I told everyone at home I was fine, because they had enough troubles.

Our English teacher, Mrs D'Souza, kept me back one day. She didn't scold. She said, "Joseph, you used to write the best essays in this class. What's happening?" I meant to say nothing. Instead, the whole thing came out, the mill, the shouting at home, how I couldn't sleep.

She listened. She told me I wasn't the only one carrying things like that. That same day she spoke to my mother, gently, and after that she let me stay after school to study where it was quiet.

The rain came down so hard the last bus from the cricket academy was forty minutes late. Karthik and Lalit sat under the tin shelter, bags between their knees.

"You've been off for weeks," Lalit said. "Missing nets, snapping at everyone."

Karthik stared at the puddles. He could say he was tired. Instead he said, "I'm not okay. Appa wants me to make the state team and top the class. I'm failing maths. I lie awake every night thinking I'm letting everyone down."

He went back to the flat and sat on the kitchen floor. Emeka came in with shopping bags and stopped. "Result?"

"Failed." Rafael rubbed his eyes. "And I'm not going to say it's fine. It's not. I'm gutted."

Dear Binita,

Hostel life in exam month is a strange animal. Half my floor lives on instant noodles and three hours of sleep. I was going that way too. Last week I skipped two dinners, slept at four, and on Thursday I sat in the exam hall and read the same question five times.

So I made myself three rules, even when I don't feel like it. Lights off by midnight. Proper meals in the mess, not noodles. And a twenty-minute walk round the campus lake after lunch, no phone.

Some days I really don't want to walk. I go anyway, slowly. It doesn't make the exams easy. But my head is clearer and I'm not crying in the corridor anymore.

Didi, you're the one who told me about the college counsellor. I haven't needed to go, but I've saved the number, and if this ever feels too heavy for too long, I will.

Your little sister,
Hansa

You want to know about that internship summer, Hafsa? Okay, so, it was bad for a bit. I'm Dhruv, and I was twenty-one, in a new city, working for a startup that emailed at midnight.

For three weeks I lived on biscuits, scrolled till two, woke at eight feeling like wet cardboard. My mood was on the floor. I kept waiting for motivation. It never came.

What worked was the boring stuff, done anyway. I set one alarm for bed, eleven thirty, and put my phone in the kitchen. I bought eggs and bread so breakfast was automatic. And I walked to the office instead of taking the metro, thirty minutes each way, even on days I didn't want to.

In ten days I felt like a person again. Not happy all the time. But steady.

And I'll say this straight: if it hadn't lifted, I'd have gone to a doctor. That's not weakness.

The sugar factory in Phaltan shut its office wing on a Monday, and Siddharth came home early carrying a cardboard box. His mother didn't ask. She put tea on.

That night he couldn't sleep. Every thought led to another: the loan on the scooter, his sister's college fees, what the neighbours would say.

At dawn he took the old calendar off the kitchen wall and turned it over. On the back he wrote a list. Collect experience letter. Visit the cooperative office about the clerk opening. Ask Jaya, his school friend now in Satara, about her company. Fix CV. Tell Aaji himself before she heard at the temple.

He circled the first item. By ten he was at the factory gate again, and by eleven the letter was in his hand, stamped.

Walking back past the tamarind trees, he noticed his chest wasn't as tight. He crossed out line one and went to find Aaji.

The warehouse in Melbourne closed with two days' notice, and Bao sat on the tram home holding his hi-vis vest, not sure why he'd kept it.

His flatmate Rafael found him at the kitchen table, staring at nothing. "Tell me what's in your head."

"Everything. Visa. Rent. My mum in Da Nang. References. Whether anyone hires forklift drivers in winter."

Rafael tore a page from the shopping pad. "Write it all down. Then circle one thing you can do tonight."

Bao wrote nine lines. He circled "Email Karen for a reference." Karen had been his shift supervisor for two years.

It took him twelve minutes. He hit send and sat back. The list was still long, but it had edges now. It wasn't a fog anymore.

"Tomorrow?" Rafael asked.

"Tomorrow, the job centre. Then I call Mum." He stuck the page on the fridge with a magnet.

qa.a: Bao wrote nine lines.

qa.q: How did Bao feel after sending the reference email?
qa.a: Bao felt calmer and more in control, because the list now had edges instead of being a fog.

Beatriz's grandmother died in March, in the small flat in Porto where she'd taught Beatriz to make rice pudding. For weeks afterwards Beatriz went to work and came home and sat in the dark.

In May her friend Hana invited her to Sunday mass at her grandmother's old parish. Beatriz wasn't sure she believed any more. She went anyway. The candles, the old ladies who hugged her and said, "Your avó talked about you every week," the same hymns her grandmother hummed while cooking; something eased.

After mass, a volunteer asked if anyone could help at the parish lunch for elderly people living alone. Beatriz stayed. She served soup to a man who kept calling her "menina". He told her about his late wife for twenty minutes.

Walking home, she cried a little. It still hurt. But it hurt in a room full of people, not alone in the dark.

qa.a: In the small flat in Porto.

qa.a: Beatriz felt comforted and less alone, hearing the old hymns and being hugged by people who knew her grandmother.

qa.q: Why might serving at the lunch have helped Beatriz?
qa.a: Helping someone else carrying grief gave her a sense of meaning and company, which made her own loss more bearable.

qa.q: What was it like for the man who talked about his late wife?
qa.a: The man may have felt listened to and less lonely, finding comfort in sharing his memories with someone kind.

grounding: An adult grieving a loved one finds comfort in ritual, community and helping others, which makes the loss more bearable.

The community kitchen at the gurdwara starts cutting onions at five in the morning. Pankaj started coming the week after his father's cremation, not because anyone asked, but because home was too quiet.

He wasn't Sikh. Nobody minded. Sabina, who ran the vegetable section, handed him a knife and a sack the first day and didn't ask questions.

For the first few mornings he chopped in silence, eyes stinging from more than onions. Then Sabina mentioned her own mother, gone two years. "Doing something for people helped me," she said. "Not instead of missing her. Alongside."

Pankaj thought of his father, who fed every stray dog on their lane. Serving dal to strangers felt, strangely, like something his father would have done.

On the tenth morning he laughed at something one of the aunties said. It surprised him. The grief was still there when he got home. But he found he could carry it.

Dear Harsha,

Thank you for coming to the bhog. I didn't get to talk to you properly, so I'm writing.

You asked how I'm doing. It's been six weeks since Mummy. The first days I couldn't eat or think. Everything felt pointless.

What's helped, a little, is the small things we keep doing. Every evening Dad and I light a diya in her corner and read one shabad she liked. I don't understand all of it, but the sound of it steadies me. On Sundays our neighbours bring food and sit with us and tell stories about her I never knew.

And I've started teaching the maths class she used to take for the kids in our lane. When they get a sum right, I hear her laugh in my head.

None of this brings her back. But it makes the days possible.

Thank you for being there.

Amandeep

For three weeks Minakshi had been crying in the office washroom. At home she stared at the ceiling until four. She forgot her niece's birthday. She stopped answering the family group.

On Saturday her brother Vaibhav dropped by with mangoes. She opened the door and couldn't speak.

"Minu?"

"I'm not managing," she said. Her voice shook. "I thought I could push through. I can't. I need proper help."

Vaibhav set the mangoes down and sat with her on the sofa. She told him everything: the new role, the sleepless nights, the heaviness in the mornings. He listened without trying to fix it.

"What do you want to do?" he asked.

"I found a counsellor near the office. I want to book it. And I want Amma and Appa to know, not find out later."

That afternoon they called their parents together. Then she booked the appointment for Tuesday, while he sat next to her.

qa.a: In the office washroom.

qa.a: Minakshi felt overwhelmed and shaky, but also clear that pushing through wasn't working and she needed proper help.

qa.a: Minakshi told her brother, called her parents and booked a counsellor; asking for help showed good judgement rather than weakness.

I'm Divyansh. For most of last year I told everyone I was fine.

I wasn't. After Nanaji died and the startup folded in the same month, I stopped sleeping properly. I snapped at people. Some mornings I sat in the car outside the office for half an hour before I could go in. I kept thinking a stronger person would handle this alone.

One Sunday my younger brother Suraj found me on the terrace at midnight, just sitting. He didn't lecture. He said, "Bhai, you're not yourself. Talk to me."

And I did. I told him I wasn't coping. Saying it out loud felt awful and then, strangely, like setting down a bag of cement.

The next morning we told Ma together. By Wednesday I'd seen a psychologist our cousin recommended. I still go every two weeks.

I used to think asking for help was weak. Now I think it was the smartest thing I did all year.
